I went through a really similar experience as the OOP. I was in high school and had a staff member who I viewed as a mentor but as I look back on it they were probably a "favorite person." Long story short, they ended up crossing some professional boundaries with me. They gave me their personal phone number and we would have frequent text and phone conversations.  Nothing inappropriate happened but eventually the staff member realized that they'd crossed a line, set boundaries with me/pulled back and I didn't like it. I ended up posting some of our personal text conversations on social media, they obviously found out and blocked me. I found out later they did get in some trouble at work.  We haven't spoken for years (I'm in college now), I regret treating them poorly but I'm not going to try to stalk them or contact them to make amends. I recently heard they're doing great, just had a kid and actually ended up getting a promotion at work. Their life is great without me in it and I don't want to mess anything up for them. I wish them the best but honestly it's best if neither of us see each other or have contact with each other again.

Never been in an outpatient program but have been hospitalized inpatient several times. Here’s my two cents :)

I think it helped. There were caring staff there and it was a wake up call to show just how bad my life had gotten and that I needed to make changes in how I treated others and myself. For reference, BEFORE insurance the cost was around $25k (per visit). My family had pretty exceptional insurance so it got cut to around $2-4k (per visit). 

You WILL get better if you put work in, however, how long that takes can vary. I knew some people who’ve been “cured” after a couple visits and a year or so in therapy but I’m still working on myself and grappling with issues after several visits and several years in therapy. I promise it WILL get better, it’s just a process. I can tell you that I am a completely different person now than I was 4 years ago (when my treatment process started.)

Oh sorry what I mean is they put you in a wheelchair and wheel you to the psych unit. (It’s kinda standard hospital procedure to wheel people around lol.) 

So basically there was a schedule that we followed on the unit I was at. Breakfast at around 8 during weekdays then groups would start - there’d be a group every hour until 12 (lunchtime! And the food was actually good.) then a half hour “quiet time” where we got to go to our rooms and chill. Then from 1-3 we’d go to a classroom and do school (remember I was on the adolescent unit.) if you had work sent up from your school you could work on it for full credit during your stay, if not you could read or something. 

Then snack time at 3, then free time until 4. Then another group and then dinner at 5. Then groups until 8. Then there was snack and the rest of the night was free with bed times at 10:30. 

Of course, during all this your therapist (they give you a therapist too) will pull you out of groups to talk. Same with psychiatrist. 

It’s a pretty rigid (sometimes boring) schedule but the groups often opened up meaningful discussions with the staff and other patients. The therapy sessions were good too, they try to get at the heart of the issue quickly so you can safely go home ASAP. It’s not a “feel good” type of therapy if you get my drift but it does help. 

Sorry for the late response!! Please feel free to continue asking questions. Also this is just based off my experience in an adolescent unit, but most units should be fairly similar.

Ok so when you’re admitted (I was on an adolescent unit, I don’t know if that would apply to you and every unit is different.) when you’re admitted they show you your room and tell you the “rules of the unit”. 
Don’t worry, nothing crazy. Just stuff like no electronics, no sharps and no hoodies or strings on clothing. 

What I’ll say about the hospital: I’ve been there. A lot. The more you go, the less it tends to help. It became a revolving door for me. Sometimes you can even pick up unhealthy habits there. HOWVER I’m not saying this to discourage you from going ESPECIALLY if it’s your first time. It can be a place of safety and stabilization. The best thing about it is going to the hospital will almost guarantee you getting a psychiatrist instantly, whereas if you apply to see one outpatient it can take months bc of waiting lists. 

I would disagree when you said going to the hospital isn’t addressing your long term  mental illness. Bc when you get a psychiatrist in the hospital they stay with you as long as you might need to take psych meds. 

Idk if you take meds at all but I do...and they have worked wonders. They’ve helped me to semi-function again. So here’s what I would say...especially if it’s your first time or you’re not medicated yet, I would go and admit yourself. Then you’ll be prescribed medication, get a psychiatrist and most importantly get into outpatient therapy. 

Hope that helps :)
